description:
Somos CYTNI, un equipo de estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas de la UNAJMA. Nos mueve la curiosidad por explorar nuevas tecnologías y convertirlas en soluciones innovadoras para distintos campos. Creemos en aprender haciendo y en que desde Andahuaylas también se puede aportar al mundo.

We are CYTNI, Systems Engineering students from UNAJMA, Peru. Driven by curiosity, we explore new technologies to build innovative solutions across many fields, believing great ideas come from anywhere.
summary:
In Andahuaylas, most families still choose what to plant the way their parents did: by watching the sky and remembering last year. But frosts now arrive at different times, the rains start late or all at once, and one bad season can leave a family without its harvest.

We built Field Shift to help with that choice. A farmer searches for their town, or clicks on a 3D globe, and sees which crops suit that place, which months bring the most risk of frost or lack of water, and what would change in an El Niño year or by 2050. The climate comes from NASA POWER, with 35 years of daily data for any point on Earth. Our reference places are Huancabamba and Pampamarca, near our university, but the app works anywhere.

The app compares at least three crop rotations, including the farmer’s current one, and explains each in plain words: why we suggest it, what supports it, what it brings to the soil, what data is missing and what to check locally. The final decision stays with the farmer, who knows their field best.
details:
Project Details
What exactly does it do?

Field Shift is a decision support system for planning crop rotations. Specifically:

It locates any place in the world by name, by GPS or with a click on a 3D globe, and gets its altitude, past climate and the weather for the coming days.
It identifies which of 125 crops suit that place based on altitude, temperature and rainfall, marking each one as suitable, suitable with care or not suitable, with the reason.
It builds a month-by-month calendar of frost, water shortage and heavy rain from 35 years of daily NASA POWER data.
It compares at least three crop rotations, including the one the farmer already uses, explaining for each one why it is suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the missing data and the risks to check locally.
It shows how those risks change in El Niño and La Niña years, and the climate trend up to 2050.
It checks the soil, the crops already grown nearby and whether the point falls in a city, a lake or a protected area, so the advice fits that exact spot.
It lets farmers add their own crops and build their own rotation.

How does it work?

The process follows a simple workflow:

Location: The farmer picks a place and the app queries several open data sources at the same time for its climate, soil, altitude and land use.
NASA Climate Data: NASA POWER returns daily maximum and minimum temperature, rainfall and solar radiation since 1991. We correct the temperature for the altitude of the field, which matters a lot in the Andes, and calculate the chance of frost and water shortage for each month.


Crop Suitability: Each crop’s requirements, taken from FAO ECOCROP and adjusted for the Andes with INIA sources, are compared with the conditions of the place.


Rotation Engine: Rotations follow farming rules that farmers already know, such as changing crop family, including legumes like broad bean or tarwi that add nitrogen to the soil, and leaving rest periods. Each rotation gets a score with its reasons.
Climate Scenarios: The NOAA ONI index identifies El Niño and La Niña years, and a CMIP6 climate model shows the trend towards 2050.
Results: Everything is shown with traffic lights, calendars and short sentences, in a simple view for farmers and a full view with all the data.

What benefits does it have?

Agricultural: Before sowing, farmers know which crops fit their land, which months need more care, and get a frost warning for the next two weeks.

Environmental: Rotations with legumes and rest periods keep the soil fertile and break the pest cycles that appear when the same crop is planted year after year.

Social: Families can prepare for an El Niño year or for warmer nights before the season starts, reducing the risk of losing a whole harvest. The app explains everything in plain words, so it is useful for people without technical training.

Economic: Seed, water and work are spent on crops with a better chance of success. The app is free, runs in a phone browser and works anywhere in the world.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to test the app with farmers from Huancabamba and Pampamarca (Andahuaylas, Peru), compare its advice with what they know about their land, and adjust the crop catalogue with their experience. In the long term, we plan to add more NASA data, such as GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and MODIS or HLS vegetation indices, so the advice reaches the level of each plot. The aim is a tool that other Andean and farming communities around the world can use.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Development Tools:Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, Obsidian (project documentation)
Infrastructure and Hosting: Streamlit Community Cloud (live app), GitHub (repository)
Web App & UI: Streamlit, Plotly, Folium, streamlit-folium, CesiumJS (3D globe), streamlit-js-eval (browser GPS)
Languages: Python, HTML, CSS, JavaScript
Data Processing: pandas, NumPy, requests
Climate & Agronomic Models: altitude-corrected temperature, monthly frost and water deficit probabilities, crop suitability scoring, rule-based rotation engine
Hardware: Development computers, smartphones for testing
Data Sources: NASA POWER, NOAA ONI, Open-Meteo (forecast, elevation, CMIP6 projection), FAO ECOCROP, ISRIC SoilGrids, SENAMHI PISCO, OpenStreetMap, SERNANP, Esri World Imagery, AWS Terrain Tiles

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

  • Claude (Anthropic): Development assistant used throughout the project. Python code generation and review for the Streamlit app, the NASA POWER data queries and the rotation engine
    • Interface design of the web app and the 3D globe
    • Debugging and error resolution during development and deployment
    • Research support to find and check open data sources (NASA POWER, FAO ECOCROP, SoilGrids, NOAA ONI)
    • Writing and translation of the app texts, help sections and project documentation (Spanish to English)
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): General questions during the hackathon, such as understanding the challenge, agronomic concepts and the data sources.
